I lived at the Morisaki Bookshop from early summer through to the beginning of the following spring.
During those months, I lived in a spare room on the second floor, practically buried in books.
The room was cramped and poorly lit, always damp and smelling of old books.
But to this day, I have never once forgotten the time I spent there.
That's because it was that place that gave me the chance to start my life for real.
If I hadn't spent those days there, my life would surely have been far more colorless, monotonous, and lonely.
A precious place, one I could never forget.
That is what the Morisaki Bookshop was to me.
Even now, those memories float vividly behind my closed eyelids.
It all started with a bolt from the blue.
Actually, for me, it was even more shocking than if frogs had started falling from the sky.
That day, Hideaki, my boyfriend of a year, suddenly said, "I'm getting married."
When I first heard it, my head was filled with nothing but question marks.
If he'd said "Let's get married," I'd have understood.
Even "I want to get married" would have meant something.
But "I'm getting married" made absolutely no sense.
Marriage is a vow made between two people; his choice of words was fundamentally wrong.
And what was with that casual tone?
He sounded as indifferent as if he'd just found a hundred yen on the sidewalk.
It was a Friday evening in the middle of June.
We were enjoying a meal at an Italian restaurant in Shinjuku after work.
The restaurant was on the top floor of a hotel, with a view of the night scenery glittering with neon lights; it was a favorite spot for both of us.
Hideaki was three years my senior at work, someone I had secretly admired ever since I joined the company.
Just being with him made my heart skip like a trampoline.
So, that night when we met alone for the first time in a while, I was drinking wine in high spirits.
But then, it happened.
I couldn't help but ask, "Huh?"
I thought I'd heard him wrong.
But he just calmly repeated himself: "So, I'm getting married next year."
"Married? Who and who?"

"Me and my girlfriend."
Wait, what?
I was still confused.
"Girlfriend?"
Then, to my disbelief, he named a girl from another department without a hint of shame.
She was in my year, a girl with such a cute aura that even another woman would want to hug her.
Compared to her, I was tall and plain-looking.
I couldn't understand why he'd even bother with me when he was already dating someone so cute.
It turned out they'd been together for two and a half years.
Which meant they'd been together much longer than we had.
I hadn't a clue he was seeing someone else. It never even crossed my mind.
I'd assumed we were keeping our relationship a secret just to avoid any awkwardness at work.
But for him, I was never the real thing—just someone to pass the time with.
Was I just blind, or was he insane?
They'd already met each other's parents and were set for the formal engagement next month.
My head was spinning.
It felt like a temple bell was ringing inside my skull.
"She's insisted on a June wedding, you see.
But there was no way we could pull it off this year, right?

So from now on..."
I just sat there, vacantly listening to the words falling from his mouth.
And I managed to mutter a single sentence: "I see. Good for you."
I was surprised the words even came out.
"Yeah, thanks!
But hey, I can still see you once in a while, Takako," Hideaki said with a grin.
It was that same carefree, athletic smile of his.
If this were a movie, I'd have probably thrown my wine in his face.
But I've always been bad at showing my feelings. I'm the type who doesn't even know what I'm thinking until I'm alone and can process everything.
Besides, that bell in my head was still ringing too loudly.
I left him in a daze and walked back to my apartment alone.
As the shock wore off, a wave of sadness hit me with terrifying speed.
The sadness far outweighed the anger.
It was a visceral sadness, so thick I felt like I could reach out and touch it.
The tears wouldn't stop.
No matter how much I wept, the feeling wouldn't fade.
I collapsed in the middle of the dark room and just cried.
I had a stupid thought—that if tears were oil, I'd be a billionaire—and then I cried even harder at how pathetic I was.
I just wanted someone to help me.
I felt it with every fiber of my being.
But I couldn't even say it out loud. All I could do was cry.
What followed was a parade of misery.
Since we worked together, I had to see him every day, whether I liked it or not.
The fact that he treated me exactly the same as always was the most painful part.
I kept running into his fiancée in the cafeteria or the break room, too.
She'd always greet me with a bright smile, whether she knew about us or not.
Soon I couldn't eat, and I couldn't sleep.
The weight fell off me. Even with makeup, my skin looked like a corpse's.
I'd burst into tears at work and have to hide in the bathroom to cry silently.
After two weeks, I hit my breaking point and handed in my resignation.
On my last day, Hideaki cheerfully told me, "Let's grab dinner sometime after you quit!"
Losing my boyfriend and my job all at once felt like being cast out into deep space.
I was from Kyushu, and since I'd only moved to Tokyo after university, most of the people I knew were from work.
I'm shy and not exactly a social butterfly, so I didn't have any close friends in the city.
Looking back, my life up until then had always been just... "so-so."

I was born into a reasonably comfortable family, went to a decent university, and got a job at a decent company. I'd expected my life to continue on that same uninspired path forever—and I was fine with that.
No great highs, but no terrible lows either.
That was the life I was meant to have.
Meeting Hideaki had been something special.
For someone as passive as me, actually being with the person I loved felt like a miracle.
Which was why the shock was so profound. I had no idea how to cope.
In the end, my only coping mechanism was sleep.
I was surprisingly tired, all the time.
Maybe it was just a way to escape reality, but as soon as I crawled under the covers, I'd drift off.
I spent days sleeping in my tiny room, a solitary pocket of space.
I suppose about a month had passed like that.
One night when I woke up, I noticed a voicemail on the phone I'd been neglecting.
I didn't recognize the number, but I listened to the message anyway.
Suddenly, a cheerful voice came through. "Hey there!"
"Takako-chan, how are things?"
It's me, Satoru!
I'm calling from the shop.
Give me a call when you can.
Oops, a customer. Gotta go.

Talk soon!"
I tilted my head in confusion.
Satoru?
Who could that be? I hadn't a clue.
Since he called me "Takako-chan," it didn't seem like a wrong number...
And what was this about a bookstore?
A bookstore.
As I replayed the word over and over in my mind, it finally clicked.
Satoru... of course, Uncle Satoru!
I remember my mother telling me a long time ago that he'd taken over the bookstore in Jinbocho that my great-grandfather had started.
I hadn't seen him in nearly ten years—not since my first year of high school—but that voice was definitely his.
A sudden chill ran down my spine.
I was certain my mother was behind this.
She was the only one I'd told about losing my job and my boyfriend. She must have asked him to check on me.
If that was the case, I knew it wouldn't be for anything good.
To be honest, I'd never really known how to handle Uncle Satoru.
He was an elusive, bohemian sort of person who did exactly as he pleased, no matter who he was with.
I'd always found his constant, strange grinning a bit off-putting.
When I was a child, I'd loved his personality. Whenever my mother took me back to her family home in Tokyo, I'd spend all my time playing in his room.
But by the time I reached adolescence, his eccentricities started to grate on me, and I began to quietly avoid him.
He'd also caused quite a stir among the relatives by suddenly getting married, despite not having a steady job at the time.
For all those reasons, I'd never once thought to visit him since moving to Tokyo. I wanted as little to do with him as possible.
The next day around noon, I reluctantly dialed his number.
I knew that if I didn't, my mother would be absolutely livid.
He'd been in his mid-twenties when I was in primary school, so he had to be well over forty now.
He picked up after just one ring.

"Hello, Morisaki Bookshop."
"Ah, it's me.

Takako."
"Oh! Takako!"
Uncle Satoru's voice boomed through the receiver.
He was as energetic as ever.
I reflexively pulled the phone away from my ear.
"It's been ages!
How are you?"
"Oh, I'm... okay."

"I knew you were in Tokyo, but you never came to visit, Takako-chan!"
"I'm sorry.

I've been busy with work."
I offered a lame excuse.
"But you've quit now, haven't you?"
He'd gone straight to the point, leaving me momentarily speechless.
It was useless to expect any tact from him.
He kept rattling on about how nostalgic it all was, before suddenly making a proposal:
"So, I was thinking—if you're not planning on working for a while, why don't you come and stay here?"
"What?"
The sudden offer caught me completely off guard.
But he didn't give me a chance to respond.
"Rent and bills must be a struggle, right?
If you stay here, everything's on the house.

Though it would be a help if you could assist a bit in the shop."
It turned out he was running the place alone and needed someone to open up in the mornings while he went for treatment for his bad back.
He lived in Kunitachi, so I'd have the place to myself after hours. He promised I'd have my privacy.
The shop had been a residence until a few years ago, so it was fully equipped with a bathroom.
I gave it some thought.
It was true that I couldn't go on like this.
My savings wouldn't last forever.
But I really didn't want anyone interfering in my life right now.
"But wouldn't I just be in the way?"
I asked, trying to find a way to decline.
But he wouldn't take no for an answer.
"Of course not!

You're more than welcome, Takako-chan!"
"But... is Aunt Momoko okay with it?"
I started to ask, then caught myself and fell silent.
I'd forgotten.
His wife, Momoko, had left him a few years back.
It had been a major scandal in the family.
My uncle had been devastated when she left. My mother had been so worried she thought he might actually make himself ill.
I'd felt sorry for him when I heard, but I'd also found it hard to believe.
They'd seemed so happy when they first married. Aunt Momoko was such a kind, gentle soul—not at all the type of person you'd expect to just disappear.
While I was lost in these thoughts, my uncle pushed ahead. "So, it's settled!"
When I tried to resist, mentioning my belongings, he told me I could store everything at the house in Kunitachi and just bring what I needed.
It felt like he'd planned everything out in advance.
"It'll be much better for you, really.

Trust me."
Trust him? How was I supposed to trust someone I hadn't seen in a decade?
"Right, I'll get things ready on this end," he said, not even waiting for my answer. Then he hung up, claiming another customer had arrived.
I just stood there, staring at the phone as the dial tone beeped in my ear.
Two weeks later, I found myself standing at Jinbocho Station.
How did I end up here?
My life was suddenly moving at a speed I could barely fathom.
When I'd spoken to my mother, she'd given me an ultimatum: either move back to Kyushu or go to Satoru's. Reluctantly, I'd chosen the latter.
I knew that if I went back to Kyushu, I'd be pushed into an arranged marriage and never see Tokyo again.
I'd worked so hard to make it to the city; going back now would feel like admitting total defeat.
I felt lightheaded, not having been out in so long.
I managed to make it to the station, and when I emerged from the subway, the midsummer heat hit me like a physical blow.
While I'd been sleeping my days away, the world had turned to summer.
The sun glared down with the intensity of a teenage boy.
When I'd quit my job, summer had felt like a distant memory.
I felt a twinge of sadness, as if even the seasons had betrayed me.
It was my very first time in Jinbocho.
My grandfather's house was in Kunitachi, so I'd never had any reason to visit this part of town.
I stood at the intersection, waiting for the light to change, and looked around.
Something felt... different.
Along the main road—Yasukuni-dori, as my uncle had called it—there was nothing but bookstores. Row upon row of them.
Everywhere I looked, there were books.
Normally, you'd think one bookstore per street would be plenty.
But here, they made up the vast majority of the shops.
There were a few large, modern stores like Sanseido and Shosen, but it was the small, weathered secondhand shops that really caught the eye.
Seeing them all huddled together like that was strangely imposing.
The large office buildings towards Suidobashi only added to the surreal atmosphere.
Puzzled, I crossed the intersection along with the lunchtime crowds and started walking down the street of bookstores.
Following my uncle's directions, I turned into a narrow alleyway called Sakura-dori.
There, too, the shops were packed with old books, as if it were the most natural thing in the world.
A secondhand book wonderland, I thought.
As I walked under the scorching sun, wondering how I'd ever find the place, I saw a man standing outside a shop, waving his arms frantically at me.
He had messy hair and thick black glasses, and he was as thin and slight as a young boy.
He was dressed in a short-sleeved plaid shirt, baggy cotton trousers, and sandals.
I definitely recognized him.
It was Uncle Satoru.

"Hey there! I knew it was you, Takako-chan!"
He gave me a wide, beaming smile.
Up close, I could see how much he'd aged.
There were deep wrinkles around his eyes, and the once-pale skin he'd shared with my mother was now covered in an incredible number of liver spots.
But the eyes behind his glasses still sparkled with a childlike intensity.
"Have you been waiting out here all this time?"
"I figured you'd be here soon.
And since this whole neighborhood is just one bookstore after another...
...I thought I'd better wait out here so you wouldn't get lost.

I've been looking for a girl in a school uniform, but you've grown up so much!"
Well, of course I had.
It had been ten years since we'd last met, at my grandfather's funeral service.
But the feeling was the same.
He was exactly as I remembered him.
Even in his forties, he still had that same carefree, detached air.
There was no one in the world less suited to the word "dignity" than him.
Back in my teens, when I was so self-conscious about how others saw me, I'd found his presence baffling and difficult to handle.
I looked away from his gaze and turned my attention to the shop.

...this is the shop my great-grandfather started."
I looked up at the sign—Morisaki Bookshop: Specialists in Modern Literature—with a strange sense of nostalgia.
I'd never met the man who started it, but it was impressive that the place had survived for three generations.
The building looked like it was at least thirty years old, if not more.
It was a small, two-story wooden building, with books visible through the glass doors, packed in tight.
"The original shop was on Suzuran-dori back in the Taisho era, so obviously that's long gone.

This is the second incarnation of the Morisaki Bookshop, you could say."
"I see."
"Anyway, come in, come in!"
My uncle practically snatched my bags and ushered me inside.
A musty scent immediately filled my nostrils.
When I remarked on the smell, he laughed and corrected me. "I prefer to think of it as the scent of a damp morning after a rainfall."
There were books everywhere.
The tiny, dimly lit shop—no more than eight tatami mats—felt as though it were steeped in the atmosphere of a bygone era.
Shelves were crammed with paperbacks and hardcovers, while massive multi-volume sets were stacked against the walls.
Even the space behind the small sales counter was overflowing.
If a major earthquake hit, there was no doubt I'd be buried alive under a literary avalanche.
"How many books are in here?"
I asked, stunned.
"Let's see...

Around six thousand, I'd say."
"Six thousand!"
I couldn't help but raise my voice in surprise.

"It's a small space, so that's about all we can fit."
"And what does "Modern Literature Specialist" actually mean?"
"Ah, we specialize in modern Japanese writers.

Take a look."
I followed his gaze, scanning the spines on the shelves.
I recognized names like Akutagawa, Soseki, and Ogai Mori, but most of them were completely unfamiliar to me.
Even the ones I knew, I'd only ever read in high school.
"You certainly have a lot of different writers here," I said. My uncle chuckled.
"Most of the shops around here have their own specialties.
Some focus on academic texts, others on playscripts.
There are even places that deal in old postcards and photographs.

This is the largest secondhand book district in the world."
"The largest in the world?"
"That's right.
It's been a hub for writers and intellectuals since the Meiji era.

It all started when schools began springing up nearby, leading to a boom in shops selling academic books."
"It goes back that far?"
"It does. This neighborhood is a place where history is still very much alive."
Writers like Ogai Mori and Junichiro Tanizaki even set their stories here.

We even get tourists from all over the world now."
He spoke with such pride, as if he'd built the place himself.
"I've lived in Tokyo all this time and had no idea," I admitted, genuinely impressed.
I was also impressed by how much my uncle knew; I'd only asked one question and he'd given me a whole lecture.
I'd always thought of him as a bit of a loafer, but he clearly knew his stuff.
I remembered his room from when I was a child being filled with dense history and philosophy books.
"You should go for a walk sometime.
There are so many fascinating spots to discover.
Anyway, that can wait. Let me show you to your room first.

The second floor is full of books, but the room itself is quite big."
When I looked inside, I nearly fainted.
His "collection" was stacked in towering pillars all over the room. There wasn't a single patch of floor visible.
It looked like some dystopian cityscape from a sci-fi film.
The ancient air conditioner was wheezing away, but it did little to stop the sweat from pouring off me.
I could hear the shrill cry of cicadas in the distance.
I shot a freezing look at my uncle.
So much for "getting things ready" for me.
Not even a mouse could have found a place to sleep in here.
"I did mean to tidy up before you got here, Takako-chan," he said, scratching his head apologetically.
"But I put my back out again three days ago.
Occupational hazard of the book trade, I suppose.
I've already moved half of it into the spare room, though.

If you just move the rest of it, you'll have plenty of space."
Just then, a customer came in downstairs. "Sorry!" he cried, practically running away.
I stood in the middle of the mess and sighed.
He'd made it sound so simple.
I felt like I'd been completely played.
But I'd already given up my apartment. I had nowhere else to go.
Resigned to my fate, I started clearing the room.
I spent the entire day wrestling with books.
Sweating and exhausted, I hauled the stacks into the next room.
If I wasn't careful, the stacks would come crashing down like the Tower of Babel. I began to harbor a growing resentment toward the things.
By evening, I'd somehow managed to move the bulk of them out.
I even managed to unearth a low table.
In the other room, the books were stacked nearly to the ceiling. I worried the floor might give way, but the building seemed sturdy enough.
I vacuumed up the dust that had been swirling around like ghosts, wiped down the walls and the tatami, and finally, the room looked like a place where a human could actually live.
I was standing at the doorway, admiring my handiwork, when my uncle came up after closing the shop.
"Oh, you've finished!
Splendid.
If you'd lived in nineteenth-century England, Takako-chan, you'd have made a formidable housemaid," he said, with his usual nonsense.
Lord, I thought. I'm going to have to live with this man.

"I'm exhausted. I'm going to bed."
"Yes, get some sleep.

I'll see you in the morning."
Once he'd gone, I took a quick bath and crawled into the musty futon without even drying my hair.
When I clicked off the light, the silence in the room was absolute.
It was as if the books in the next room were swallowing every sound.
I stared blankly at the dim ceiling, a wave of loneliness washing over me. "I don't think I can ever get used to this place," I thought.
But the feeling lasted only a moment.
A second later, I was already sound asleep.
In my dream, I was an android housemaid in a city of the near future.
Every building in the city was constructed from old books.
When I woke up the next morning, I had no idea where I was.
I glanced at the alarm clock by my side; the hands were already pointing to 10:22.
Reality came rushing back, and I bolted upright. "Oh no!"
The shop was supposed to open at ten.
I'd set my alarm for eight, but somehow I'd turned it off in my sleep.
Who could have done such a thing? Me, obviously.
It was a total disaster.
I'd always prided myself on being a morning person; in three years at my old job, I'd never been late a single day.
Still in my pajamas, my hair a total mess, I raced downstairs and hauled up the heavy shutter.
Summer sunlight flooded into the shop.
Every other shop on the street was already open. I was late—completely and utterly late.
What was I going to do? How could I possibly explain this to my uncle?
I sat at the counter in my pajamas for half an hour, paralyzed with panic.
But to my surprise, not a single soul came in.
Even as time passed, there was no sign of a customer.
People walked by on the street outside, but they all passed the shop without so much as a glance.
Feeling like an idiot, I went back upstairs, took my time getting dressed, brushed my hair, and even put on a bit of makeup before heading back down.
It wasn't until around noon that people finally started to trickle in.
But most of them just picked up a fifty- or hundred-yen paperback.
I started to wonder how the shop could possibly survive like this.
I must have stifled thirty yawns and nodded off at least twice.
Around one, a stocky man with a shining bald head walked in.
He took one look at me sitting at the counter and said, "Oh?"
"Where's Satoru? And who are you, exactly?
A part-timer?
I didn't think this place could afford to hire anyone."

He was a remarkably overfamiliar old man.
"Um, my uncle should be here around two."
"I'm Takako, his niece.

"Well now, I had no idea Satoru had such a lovely young niece!"
I gave him a polite smile.
I was just glad he hadn't seen me earlier in my pajamas.
He seemed like a decent enough fellow.
He looked kindly, and more importantly, he clearly had good taste.
"So, I was thinking of re-reading some Naoya Shiga.
My wife got rid of most of my copies, you see."
He chatted away as he wandered through the stacks.
I hadn't a clue what he was talking about, considering we'd only just met.
"So, where are they?"
"Where are what?"

"The Shiga books, of course!"
"Oh, right.

Um, they're probably somewhere around here..."
The man suddenly fixed me with a sharp, appraising look.
"Do you read?"
"No, not really," I said with a smile. Immediately, his expression changed to one of absolute horror.
His eyes flashed.
And that was the start of his lecture.
Good grief.
Young people today don't read. It's all computers and games. It's a tragedy.
And even if they do read, it's just manga or those flimsy cell phone novels.
My own son is nearly thirty and he does nothing but play video games.
Listen to me, young lady.
If you don't read, you'll only ever see the surface of the world.

"How was your day? Any trouble?"

"No," I said, exhausted.

"But a man came in earlier—he had a head like a dandelion that's lost all its fluff except for the sides—and he talked my ear off."
"Ah, that's Sabu-san.

I couldn't help but give a wry smile.
The name Sabu-san seemed to suit him perfectly.

"What's that?"

Even people your age.
To them, this place is like heaven.

Your room was certainly full of them, Uncle.
How long has it been since you took over the shop?"

About ten years now, I suppose.
Though compared to some of the others around here, I'm still a rank amateur.

It's a world I can't even imagine."

I just gave him a noncommittal laugh.
I managed to get through the next few days without oversleeping.
Luckily, the mornings were usually quiet, so I could just sit behind the counter and let my mind wander.
Moving into the bookshop hadn't really changed my life all that much.
I'd open up in the morning, mind the shop until my uncle arrived, and then I was free.
I'd trudge back upstairs and crawl back into bed.
The room was sparsely furnished, barely a living space at all, but that suited me just fine.
Truth be told, I wanted nothing more than to shut out the rest of the world.
Uncle Satoru would always show up after noon, dressed in the kind of casual clothes that would never fly in a corporate office.

According to him, his ability to keep the shop stocked depended heavily on his connections and this professional network.

"That's right.

After that, I was as silent as a grave, no matter what he said.

I was sure my mother had told him at least some of what I'd been through.
The fact that he didn't seem to care at all made me furious.
To make matters worse, even Sabu-san started teasing me about my sleeping habits, calling me "Takako-chan the Sleeping Demon."
"Who told you that?"
I asked him, annoyed.
I knew exactly who was responsible.
What a frustrating man he was.

"I don't know how you can sleep for fifteen hours a day."
"I don't sleep for fifteen hours.

It's more like thirteen."
When I snapped back at him, Sabu-san just shook his head.

"When I was your age, I'd stay up all night reading."
"When I decide to sleep, I sleep."
"That stubbornness is just like Satoru's."
"No it isn't! Who'd want to be like that idiot?"
"That sharp tongue of yours is just like his, too," Sabu-san said with a chuckle.

"We are nothing alike. Don't even start."
"Now, now.

Don't underestimate the man," Sabu-san said, his voice suddenly grave. "He might be an idiot, but he's the savior of this shop."
"Savior?"
I stared at him in disbelief.

"It's true. You should ask him about it sometime."
He gave me a mysterious look, waved a hand, and walked out with a jaunty "Adios!"
I didn't care.
I wasn't the least bit interested in whether my uncle was a savior or not.
My only desire was to crawl back into my futon and sleep.
I was so tired I was starting to annoy even myself.
I'd told Sabu-san thirteen hours, but on my days off I'd sleep for twenty-four.
I wanted to sleep until there was nothing left of me but sleep.
In my dreams, the pain couldn't reach me.
My dreams were like sweet, golden honey.
And like a honeybee, I sought them out, losing myself in their sweetness.
Being awake, on the other hand, was unbearable.
I couldn't stop thinking about Hideaki, no matter how hard I tried.
The way he laughed, the way he'd run his fingers through my hair.
I loved everything about him—his selfishness, the way he was so self-conscious about being tone-deaf, his unexpected tenderness.
I knew I was being an idiot, but I'd been happy with him. Those memories were etched into my very soul, and they refused to fade.
Even now, I found myself wondering if everything he'd said to me that night had been a lie.
Maybe he'd just been teasing me.
Maybe he was just waiting to say, "Gotcha!"
But I knew that wasn't true.
If it were, I wouldn't be here.
So I kept on sleeping, determined to drown out the thoughts.
Time slipped away from me, faster than I could grasp.
"Takako-chan, you awake?"
One evening at the tail end of summer, my uncle called to me through the door.
I looked at the clock; it was eight, and the shop was closing.
"I'm asleep," I called back from under the covers.

"People who are asleep don't answer back."
"But I am."

I am the Sleep Demon, after all."
My uncle laughed on the other side of the door.

"Are you still mad about what I told Sabu-san?"
"Of course I am.

You made me sound like a monster."
"Now, now.
I was only worried about you.
He's always asking about you. Look, why don't you come out for a bit?
There's somewhere I want to go. Want to come with me?"
"No thanks," I said flatly.
But he wouldn't let it go.
"It'll be good for you. I promise.

If you come, I'll never bother you about your sleeping again. Deal?"
"Really?"
I asked, skeptical.
"Pinky swear.

If I'm lying, you can flick my forehead three hundred times."
I reluctantly got up, ran my fingers through my hair, and opened the sliding door a crack.

"Is that a promise?"
I glared at him through the gap in the door, and he nodded, smiling.

"I promise."
The place he had in mind was only a stone's throw from the bookshop.
"We're here," he said, stopping in front of a building in a back alley.
It was an old wooden coffee shop, the sort of place that's hard to find these days.
It looked exactly like the kind of place where you'd expect to find a dapper, middle-aged man with a mustache behind the counter.
A sign reading "Suboru" glowed softly in the darkness.
"This is my local," my uncle said. He pushed open the heavy door, and the rich aroma of coffee wafted out to meet us.
"Oh, Satoru-san.
Welcome!" The man at the counter, busy pouring water into a coffee siphon, looked up as we entered.
"Evening, Master.

This is my niece, Takako-chan."
"Hello," I said. I sat down next to my uncle at the small counter and gave a polite bow.
The master didn't have a mustache, but he had a sharp, distinguished face and an air of quiet dignity.
He looked to be in his late forties.
I wished my uncle, who was still such a child at heart, would take a leaf out of his book.
"I'll have the house blend.
And for you, Takako-chan?"
"I'll have the same," I said, looking around the shop.
The interior was bathed in the soft glow of lanterns, and with a gentle piano piece playing in the background, the atmosphere was incredibly peaceful.
The dark brick walls were covered in messages and drawings left by past customers.
It all blended perfectly with the shop's warm, inviting feel.
I felt a rare spark of excitement; there was something truly special about this place.
I could feel some of my energy starting to return.
"This place has been here for about fifty years.
All sorts of famous people used to hang out here," my uncle explained.
"I can see why. You can't just manufacture an atmosphere like this," I said, nodding.
Five minutes later, a young waitress brought our coffee.

"Good evening, Morisaki-san."
"Hi, Tomo-chan.

This is my niece, Takako-chan."
"Hello," I said. Tomo-chan gave me a bright smile and a warm "Good evening."
"Tomo-chan is a regular at the bookshop.

She's a real bookworm."
"Not really," she said, smiling shyly.
She looked to be about my age, maybe a little younger.
She had soft, round cheeks and a gentle way of speaking.
She looked very sweet in her black apron.
I had a feeling we'd get along, which made me happy.
"What is it, Takako-chan?
Do you only like girls?
We have a young man here, too." My uncle waved a hand toward the back of the counter.

"Takano-kun!"
"Hello, Morisaki-san." A tall, lanky young man poked his head out from behind the curtain and greeted my uncle.

"Takano-kun, you should take my niece out on a date sometime!"
"Hey!"
I gave my uncle's hand a sharp slap.
Takano-kun seemed incredibly shy; he turned beet-red at the suggestion.
"Takano-kun is apprenticing here. He wants to open his own place one day.

But he's always messing up and getting scolded by the master."
My uncle seemed to take great delight in that last part.
"Don't make me sound like a monster," the master chimed in immediately.
I felt sorry for the guy, but he was so thin he looked like a stiff breeze would knock him over. I could see why he might get scolded.
My uncle was in high spirits for the rest of the evening.
When a middle-aged woman nearby called out his name, he practically wagged his tail as he hurried over. "Mrs. Shibamoto!" he cried, before flitting off to another table a moment later.
He was professional enough in the shop, but out here he was a different person entirely.
I felt like a dog owner being dragged around by a particularly excitable pet.
"Satoru is something of a celebrity in these parts," the master said with a wry smile.
Kind wrinkles crinkled around his eyes as he spoke.
"He certainly has a lot of energy," I said, not without a touch of irony.
"But honestly, this is the best coffee I've ever had.

And your shop is just beautiful."
The master gave a low, quiet chuckle.
"Thank you.
I think young people find a place like this refreshing if they've never seen anything like it before.
Takako-san, was it?
Is this your first time in the neighborhood?"
"Yes, my very first time.

But I've just moved into my uncle's shop."
"Ah, the Morisaki Bookshop.
That's wonderful.

I hope you enjoy your time in Jinbocho."
"We'll see," I said with a grimace.
"What's wrong?"

"My uncle says the exact same thing."
"Well, of course he does.

No one loves this town more than Satoru."
"I don't really get it," I said, sighing.
"But I wasn't lying about your shop. It's lovely.

I'd love to come back."
"Please, you're welcome anytime," the master said with a warm smile.
We stayed for a long time, and the night was late when my uncle and I finally left the shop and began to stroll down the street.
There was a definite chill in the air; autumn was beginning to make itself felt.
My uncle seemed to have been affected by his single beer, and he staggered along in front of me, muttering about what a beautiful night it was.
It occurred to me that I hadn't walked with him like this since I was a little girl.
We used to spend whole days together, holding hands and "exploring" the area around my grandfather's house.
I wonder what I found so exciting back then.
I remember laughing and running around with such joy.
As an only child and a shy one at that, my uncle had felt like the kind older brother I never had. I used to look forward to seeing him more than anything.
As I walked, memories of us singing Beatles songs together to his clumsy guitar playing, or of me being lost in his collection of manga, came flooding back with startling clarity.
I felt a sudden twinge of the same affection I'd felt for him all those years ago.
"Hey, Uncle Satoru," I said, calling out to his retreating back.
"Yeah?"
He turned around, his eyes still sparkling with that same boyish light.
"What were you doing when you were my age?"

"Let's see... I think I spent most of my time reading."
"Is that it?"
I was a bit disappointed.

"That doesn't sound very different from how you are now."
"And I traveled."
"Traveled?"
"Yeah. I'd work part-time, save up some money, and then go.
I traveled all over the place with just a backpack.
Thailand, Laos, Vietnam, India, Nepal.

I even backpacked across Europe once."
I was stunned to learn he'd been so adventurous.
"Why did you do all that?
Didn't you ever want a normal job?"
"Well..." He crossed his arms and looked thoughtful, as if he were back in those days.
"In short, I wanted to see the world for myself.
I wanted to find out what I was capable of.

I wanted to know what it meant to live a life that was truly mine, and no one else's."
It seemed a bit contradictory to me—all that traveling just to end up running a small bookstore.
I couldn't help but wonder.
The story was a far cry from the image I'd had of him when I was young.
But now that I was an adult, I could almost understand how he felt.
In university, I'd often dreamed of living a life that was true to my own values, free from any outside expectations.
But I'd never had the courage to actually do anything about it.
Maybe that was the secret to his easy, carefree nature.
I felt a twinge of envy.
"Yeah, I spent my twenties just drifting around.
My father was always on my back about it.

Then my father fell ill and passed away, and I just sort of fell into running the shop."
"Do you ever regret it?"
"Not for a second," he said, laughing.
"I can't imagine a better job for me.
For a book lover, there's no place on earth like this town.
I'm proud to be a part of it.

I owe everything to my father and grandfather."
"I see."

"That must be nice, Uncle."
"What must?"
He looked at me, puzzled.

"Doing what you love and making a living from it."
"It wasn't always that simple.
I resisted it at first, in my own way.
I never imagined I'd end up following in my father's footsteps.
I still have my doubts, even now.
But I suppose figuring out what you really want takes time.

Maybe it's something you only truly understand at the end of your life."
"I... I feel like I'm just wasting my time like this..."
My uncle looked at me and gave a gentle smile.
"I don't think so.
Sometimes it's important to just stop for a while.
Think of it as a rest stop on the long journey of life.
You're a ship that's pulled into a harbor to drop anchor for a bit.

When you're ready, you can set sail again."
"And yet you're the one complaining that I sleep too much," I said, a little defensively.
He let out a loud laugh.

"We humans are full of contradictions, aren't we?"
I couldn't help but laugh.
That was just like him.
"So, did you learn everything you know from traveling and reading?"
"I suppose so.
But the more I traveled and the more I read, the more I realized how little I actually knew. I felt like I hadn't really seen anything at all.
That's just life, I guess.
We spend our whole lives trying to find our way.
Like that poem by Santoka.

"No matter how far I go, the green mountains still lie ahead."
"Hey, Uncle."
I decided to ask him something that had been on my mind for a while, emboldened by the momentum of the moment.
"Yeah?"
"Why did Aunt Momoko leave you?"
"Well...
We were very much alike, she and I.
I think that's what brought us together, and in the end, it was what drove us apart.
We met on a journey and fell in love.
But a journey has to end eventually.
You have to pull into a port at some point.

I thought we were headed for the same place, but I was wrong."
"I see...
How did you feel? Were you heartbroken?"
"Well..." He looked up at the cloudy night sky.
"I was sad, of course.

But..."
"But?"

"But now, I just want her to be happy, wherever she is."
"But..." I said, not quite understanding.
"She left you, didn't she?"
"But Momoko was the only woman I ever really loved.
That won't ever change.
The time we spent together is still a part of me.

In that way, I'll always love her."
How could he feel like that?
I wanted to ask, but he looked so small and lonely standing there under the streetlight that I couldn't bring myself to say another word.
That night, I found I couldn't sleep.
I lay in my futon, my mind racing with a million different thoughts until I felt like my head was going to explode.
Thoughts of the future and bitter memories of the past kept me awake, a heavy weight on my chest.
This is no good.
I sat up suddenly.
If I didn't do something, the anxiety was going to swallow me whole.
I considered watching TV, but I would have had to move all those books again just to see the screen.
Besides, it was three a.m. There was nothing to watch anyway.
If only I had something to read, I thought, staring into the dark.
Anything to help pass the time.
Then it hit me.
I was living in a bookstore, for heaven's sake.
I was surrounded by books.
I'd been so annoyed by them that I'd completely forgotten what they were actually for.
I switched on the light and started looking for something—anything—that looked halfway interesting.
But I had no idea where to start.
They all just looked like old, dusty relics.
My uncle would probably have known exactly what to pick.
Resigned, I stood before a stack of paperbacks and closed my eyes.
I reached out and pulled one at random from the pile.
The title was "Until a Certain Girl's Death."
By Saisei Muro.
I remembered the name from high school.
In the dim light of my bedside lamp, I crawled back under the covers and started to read, not expecting much.
I figured I'd be asleep in ten minutes.
But something happened.
An hour later, I was completely hooked.
The language was a bit old-fashioned in places, but the themes of human nature were universal, and the story spoke to me in a way I hadn't expected.
It was about a boy growing up in Kanazawa, his move to Tokyo to become a poet, and his life in Nezu.
There were stories of his complicated feelings for the women in his life—his half-sister, a friend's girlfriend.
The "certain girl" was someone he'd met by chance while living in poverty in the city.
Their connection had brought a brief moment of healing to his troubled soul.
What I loved most was the sense of quiet kindness that permeated the entire book, despite the protagonist's difficult circumstances.
There was a gentle, almost indescribable emotion that pulled at my heartstrings.
It felt like a profound love for life itself, coming through the pages.
I looked up to find the sky starting to lighten.
But I couldn't stop reading.
The next morning, I was waiting for Uncle Satoru, still buzzing with excitement.
He looked stunned to see me actually running toward him to say hello.
"This book was amazing," I said, showing him my copy of "Until a Certain Girl's Death."
And then, his face lit up.
He beamed at me.
Like a child on his birthday.
"Yeah, it was really good.
It really... it really moved me." I felt frustrated that I couldn't find the right words to describe it.
The word "moved" didn't even begin to cover the complexity of what I was feeling.
"I'm so glad to hear you say that, Takako-chan.

And starting with Saisei Muro! You've got excellent taste."
Seeing him so genuinely happy made me feel a surge of happiness, too.
We spent a long time talking about the book after that.
There's a special kind of joy in finding a connection with someone you thought you had nothing in common with.
Even if it was just my uncle—or perhaps especially because it was him—it was a wonderful feeling.
Sometimes, the smallest thing can open a door you never knew was there.
That's exactly how it felt for me.
That was the spark. After that, I started devouring books one after another.
It was as if a long-dormant hunger for reading had suddenly woken up.
I couldn't get enough.
I read slowly, savoring every word.
I had all the time in the world, and a seemingly endless supply of books at my fingertips.
Kafu Nagai, Junichiro Tanizaki, Osamu Dazai, Haruo Sato, Ryunosuke Akutagawa, Koji Uno...
Names I'd heard but never read, names I'd never heard of—I picked up anything and everything that looked interesting and read with a newfound greed.
And yet, the more I read, the more I found to read.
I'd had no idea that reading could be such a transformative experience.
I felt as though I'd been missing out on something vital all my life.
I stopped spending my days in bed.
I didn't feel the need to hide from the world anymore.
Instead of sleeping, I'd finish my shift and head straight to my room or a nearby cafe with a book.
I discovered that old books were full of hidden histories.
And I don't just mean the stories they told.
Every volume bore the traces of the years it had lived through.
In a copy of Motojiro Kajii's "A Certain Landscape of the Heart," I found a passage that stopped me in my tracks:
To see—that is already something in itself.

It is to have a part, or even the whole, of one's soul pass into the thing seen.

Underneath those words, a previous reader had drawn a firm line in ink.
I'd been moved by those same words, and seeing that line made me feel a sudden, strange connection to that unknown person.
Sometimes, I'd find a bookmark made from a pressed flower.
I'd catch a faint, ghostly scent of the bloom and find myself wondering who had placed it there, and what they had been thinking at that exact moment, so many years ago.
It was the kind of connection across time that you can only find in a secondhand book.
I found myself growing more and more fond of the Morisaki Bookshop.
Spending my days in that quiet, time-worn space started to feel like a rare and precious gift.
I learned more about the writers on our shelves, and I even started to get to know the regulars.
Even Sabu-san noticed the change in me. "Well now, Takako-chan," he said, "you're starting to look like you know what you're doing."
Exploring the neighborhood became another part of my new routine.
The weather had turned cool, making it the perfect time for long walks.
Watching the leaves on the trees turn gold day by day felt like a reflection of the slow, quiet changes happening in my own heart.
I saw the town with completely different eyes than I had on that first day.
Jinbocho felt like a world of adventure, and I found myself looking forward to every walk.
There were so many hidden gems—tucked away bookstores, cozy cafes, quirky little bars that I found myself wanting to explore.
And despite the activity, there was a unique sense of peace about the place. It lacked the harsh, modern edge that I'd always found so draining.
I realized, too, that every bookstore had its own distinct personality.
Some specialized in foreign literature, others in historical novels. There were shops dedicated to old movie magazines, children's books, even ancient Edo-period manuscripts.
The owners were just as varied—some were gruff and traditional like my grandfather, others were young and welcoming.
I stopped by a local information center and learned that there were over a hundred and seventy bookstores in the area alone.
My uncle hadn't been exaggerating. It really was the greatest book district in the world.
Whenever my feet grew tired, I'd duck into a cafe for a rest.
A cup of hot coffee was the perfect end to a long walk in the crisp air; it warmed me to my very soul.
And so I spent the deepening days of autumn.
My new life was doing wonders for my state of mind.
I could feel the knots in my heart slowly, gently beginning to untie.
I started making friends in the neighborhood, too.
I became a regular at Suboru and got to know the staff, especially a waitress named Tomo-chan.
Tomo-chan was a graduate student in Japanese literature and worked at the cafe part-time.
She'd often drop by the bookshop as a customer, as well.
She was two years younger than me.
She had a quiet, gentle demeanor, but beneath the surface lay a fierce passion for literature.
Her love for the writers she studied was truly remarkable.
I found her warmth and enthusiasm incredibly endearing.
Before long, she started coming by the shop even when she didn't need anything. We'd sit together on the second floor, drinking tea and surrounded by books.
"Oh, this is just a dream!" she'd cried when she first saw my room, her face lighting up.
"Really?
It's pretty small.
And there's only the one gas ring." I couldn't help but be practical about the place I called home.
"But that's the whole point!" she said, looking at me as if I were missing something obvious.
"It's so simple. No clutter, just you and all these books.

What could be better?"
"I suppose you're right," I said.
"I know I am!" She leaned in, her eyes shining.
I looked around the room.
It was funny how her enthusiasm made the once-drab room feel suddenly full of charm.
At her suggestion, we bought some cosmos from the florist on the corner and put them in a vase on my little table.
The flowers seemed to brighten the whole room.
From that day on, I always made sure to have some fresh flowers in the room.
One day, after we'd become good friends, I asked her something I'd been curious about.
"Tomo-chan, how did you get so into books?"
She answered in her usual soft, gentle tone.
"Well...
In middle school, I was painfully shy. I was terrified of what people would think if I spoke my mind, so I hardly said a word.
But inside, I was full of all these dark, complicated feelings. I hated myself for it; I felt so ugly...
Then I found a copy of Dazai's "Schoolgirl" that belonged to my sister. That was where it all started.

Now, I'm completely hooked."
"I see.
I guess everyone who loves books has that one story that changes everything for them," I said, genuinely moved.

"I hope we both find lots more wonderful books to love," she said with a smile.
"Me too," I said, nodding firmly.
It was around that time that something unexpected happened involving Tomo-chan.
One afternoon, while I was working in the shop alone, Takano-kun from Suboru suddenly appeared.
I'd never really spoken to him before, since he was always busy in the kitchen, but he was certainly hard to miss with that lanky frame of his.
I recognized him right away. "Hello," I said.
He gave me a stiff little bow and a mumbled "Hello," then started glancing around the shop, looking incredibly nervous.
I thought he was acting a bit odd. "Are you looking for anything in particular?" I asked.
"No, I... no, not really..." he stammered.
He was acting very strangely. His face was bright red.
He looked for all the world like a boy trying to talk to his crush.
Then it dawned on me.
Wait... did he have a crush on *me*?
I remembered how flustered he'd gotten when my uncle had joked about us going on a date.
Could it be?
The thought made me feel suddenly very self-conscious.
A long, awkward silence followed.
The tension in the room was so thick I could barely breathe.
Just as I was bracing myself to say something, he burst out: "Um!"
I practically jumped.
I was certain a confession was coming. My mind was already racing, trying to figure out how to turn him down gently.
But what he actually said was the last thing I expected.
"Ms. Aihara... she comes here quite a bit, doesn't she?"
He was beet-red as he said it.
"Ms. Aihara? You mean Tomo-chan?"

"Yes."
"Yeah, she comes by during her lunch breaks sometimes. Why?"
"What... what do you talk about?"
My face went cold in an instant.
I want my anxiety back, I thought, feeling like an idiot.
So you have a thing for Tomo-chan?"
I couldn't help but needle him a bit.

"No, it's not... it's not that..."
"It's fine, it's fine.
She's a very cute girl.
But surely you'd know her better than I do, working in the same place?"
"No, I'm stuck in the kitchen, and she's out in the front.

And I'm... I'm not very good at talking to people."
"I see.

So you're just as shy as you look."
"Do you... do you think she has a boyfriend?"
He asked with such gravity, as if the fate of the world depended on the answer.
"I have no idea.
I've never actually asked her.
But she's such a lovely girl, inside and out.

It wouldn't surprise me if she did."
"Could you... could you maybe find out for me? Casually?"
"Why should *I* ask her?

Ask her yourself."
"But you're friends! You could just bring it up naturally, right?"

"And I've... I've never actually talked to a girl first."
"You're talking to me right now," I said, stunned.
Did he not even see me as a woman?
However, he didn't even seem to hear me.
"I'll make it worth your while.
If you help me, I'll pay for all your coffees from now on." At that, all my annoyance vanished. I was all ears.
"Really?
I'll be there every day!"

"Maybe not every day..."
"Don't be so cheap!
It's a small price to pay for the girl of your dreams, isn't it?"
"I suppose..." he said, looking a little defeated.

"But you have to promise not to tell her. Ever."
"I know, I know," I said, patting my chest.
And so, our secret pact was formed.
It turned out he'd had a crush on her for almost six months.
But in all that time, he'd never said more than a simple "hello" to her, contenting himself with admiring her from afar.
It was a bit pathetic, in a way, but also strangely sweet.
Now that I was involved, I decided I might as well try to help them get together.
It was probably none of my business, but he seemed like a good guy, despite the shyness.
There was no harm in giving him a little nudge.
So, purely for the sake of young love—and not at all for the free coffee—I set to work.
I started by trying to get as much information as I could out of Tomo-chan.
I found out she was single and didn't have anyone special in her life.
Her favorite color was navy blue.
She loved dormice.
And her favorite place in the world was Jinbocho, of course.
I soon became an expert on all things Tomo-chan, though I think I started to weird her out a little bit with all my questions.
Every time I had a new piece of information, I'd head over to Suboru for my free coffee and brief Takano-kun.
"Apparently, her favorite animal is the dormouse," I'd whisper over the counter. "Wow... that's... that's incredible," he'd whisper back.
The master, who turned out to be a bit of a gossip, saw us whispering and started telling everyone that we were dating.
But for all my hard work, things weren't really progressing.
Takano-kun was too terrified to actually talk to her, so they were at a complete standstill.
He'd been thrilled just to know she was single, but at this rate, it was going to take a decade before they even had a proper conversation.
I had to do something.
I was getting frustrated on their behalf.
I tried to think of a way to get them in the same room together.
Then, the perfect opportunity presented itself.
One afternoon, while Tomo-chan and I were having tea, she mentioned the upcoming secondhand book festival.
"A secondhand book festival? What's that?"
I asked, intrigued.
"You don't know, Takako-san?
Every autumn, the bookstores around here hold a massive outdoor sale.

The whole of Jinbocho gets packed. It's incredible."
"Really?

That sounds like fun."
"Your uncle's shop participates, of course."
"Really? He never mentioned it."
"Every shop does!" Honestly, my uncle was useless when it came to important information.
I made a mental note to give him a piece of my mind later.
"I was planning on going this year. Would you like to come with me?"
I had a sudden brainwave.
This was the perfect chance.
I had to tell Takano-kun.
I agreed immediately. "I'd love to!"
The Kanda Secondhand Book Festival began in late October and lasted for a week.
The streets were lined with carts and shelves overflowing with books, like a giant open-air market.
The festival was a huge success.
People of all ages and backgrounds flocked to the town, all united by a love of books.
It was far busier than I'd imagined. Yasukuni-dori and Sakura-dori were buzzing with energy from early in the morning.
It was a truly impressive sight.
Our shop was right in the middle of it all.
Uncle Satoru and I had spent days sorting through stacks of books to put out on the carts in front of the shop.

When I told him I was leaving, my uncle was stunned. "You don't have to decide so suddenly..." he said, clearly flustered.
But I had already made up my mind.
"I've enjoyed my long vacation from life for quite a while now.

If I don't set out to find my own place soon, I'll end up gaining nothing."
After hearing that, my uncle said no more.
During my final month at the Morisaki Bookshop, I savored every moment.
I put my heart into my work and read as much as I could.
I gave the shop and the upstairs room a thorough cleaning as a gesture of gratitude.

I even went back to the room where I'd haphazardly piled the books on my first day and organized them with care.
I told the regulars and the staff at Suboru that I was leaving.
Everyone seemed so genuinely sad to see me go that it almost made me cry, realizing how much I'd come to be cared for.
Sabu-san even joked, "Come and marry my son," and seemed half-serious about setting us up.
Takano-kun and Tomo-chan even threw a small farewell party for me.
We shared a hot pot on the second floor of the shop and hung out late into the night.
Tomo-chan was genuinely sad to lose her reading companion. "Let's go to the festival together again next year," she promised.
Takano-kun told me in confidence that he had recently taken Tomo-chan to a movie in Shibuya.
They weren't quite dating yet, but for someone as shy as him, it was massive progress.
I felt a surge of joy for him and shouted, "That's great!"
and couldn't help but give his thin back a hearty slap.
Later, I unexpectedly heard from Hideaki's fiancée, Murano-san, and we met at a cafe to talk.
What weighed on me most was that I had caused her so much trouble that night.
I went to our meeting fully prepared to apologize as profusely as I could.
However, as soon as we sat down, she was the one who gave me a deep, sincere bow.
She had been suspicious of his behavior for a while, and my presence that night had confirmed her fears. She had questioned him until he finally confessed everything.
She told me she had never even dreamed that I was the one he'd been seeing until that night.
Murano-san apologized over and over, and even when I told her I was also to blame, she just kept shaking her head.
She had decided to call off the wedding entirely.

When I tried to apologize again, she stopped me. "It's not your fault, Takako-san," she said firmly.
I still felt a lingering sense of guilt, but when I told my uncle about it later, he just said, "She's doing the right thing.
Better to find out what a loser he is now than after they're married."

It was a typical response for someone who despised Hideaki as much as my uncle did, but I had to admit there was some truth to it. I felt a weight lift from my shoulders.

On my last night at the shop, my uncle and I sat on the second-floor balcony, drinking coffee and gazing up at the winter sky.
As a parting gift, he gave me a massive stack of secondhand books.
He said they were all stories that had deeply moved him when he was young.
Peering into the heavy paper bag, I saw it was filled with works by authors I'd come to appreciate, like Takehiko Fukunaga and Kazuo Ozaki.
We spent that final night in a state of quiet, comfortable ease.
And I know I will never forget the words he said to me then.
He started by saying, "There's one thing I want you to promise me," and then he said this:
"Don't ever be afraid to love people.
While you're still young, I want you to love as many people as you can.
Even if it ends in sadness, please don't live a life where you never love anyone. That's a lonely way to be.
I was so worried that this experience would make you close yourself off to love forever.
Loving someone is a beautiful thing.
Please, never forget that.
The memory of loving someone never truly leaves you.
It stays with you, keeping your heart warm for the rest of your life.

When you get to be my age, you'll understand what I mean."
He looked at me and asked, "So, can you promise me that?"
he asked.
"I understand.
I promise," I said, nodding.
"I think I've already learned that here, thanks to you.

So you don't need to worry about me."
"I see.

Then I know you'll be just fine, wherever you go."
"Yeah.

Thank you, Uncle."

On the morning I left, I stood in the early morning sunlight and took one last long look at the Morisaki Bookshop.
It was just a small, old wooden building.
It felt almost impossible to believe that I had actually lived there.
I stood there for a long time, my breath blooming white in the air. The street was bathed in soft morning light.
None of the shops were open yet, and the air was filled with a quiet, indescribable peace.
I straightened my posture and gave a deep, formal bow toward the shop.
I vowed to never forget the lessons I'd learned during my time at the Morisaki Bookshop.
I also gave my sincere thanks to my uncle, who had come out so early to see me off.
He had become such a massive presence in my life.
It was strange to think that when I first arrived, I could never have imagined feeling this way.
When it came time to say goodbye, his tough act from the night before vanished completely, and he started sobbing like a child.
"I've changed my mind, I don't want you to go!

Don't leave me, Takako-chan!"
He gripped my hand tightly and wouldn't let go.
"I'll come visit you all the time," I said, comforting him, even though it felt like our roles were reversed.
"So please, take care of yourself.

And keep this shop safe for me."
I knew that if I stayed even a second longer, my own resolve would crumble.
So I quickly said my final goodbye and started walking down the street.
I marched all the way to the end of Sakura-dori without looking back once.
As I walked, the memories flooded my heart, and tears began to sting my eyes.

But I fought them back until I reached the end of the road.
I had a sudden premonition and stopped, slowly turning around.
There was my uncle, a small figure in the distance, standing in the middle of the road and waving frantically.
Seeing him like that, I couldn't hold it in anymore.
The tears came pouring out, uncontrollably.
With my face crumpled and wet with tears, I waved back with all my might.
He responded by waving even harder.
The morning sun was shining brightly behind him.
"Take care of yourself!" I shouted.
I turned on my heel and began walking down Yasukuni-dori, which was already starting to fill with people.
The people passing by probably thought I was a strange woman, walking along and sobbing like that.
But I didn't care at all.
Because I was crying because I wanted to, and these were the happiest tears I had ever shed in my life.
In the crisp early morning air, there was the faintest hint of spring.
And I walked straight ahead into it, without looking back.
